evidence: Traupman 53: excursiōnem … facere, go on an outing (a picnic)
terms.comment: Pliny’s word for a landowner’s frequent trips out to see to his estates. Its commoner classical sense is military, a sally or a raid (Caes., Liv.); the context keeps the two apart. Traupman uses it of an outing.

terms.gloss: make a short trip, run over to a place
terms.grammar: perfect also excurrī; with in or the bare name of a town
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.45.2: ut Puteolōs excurrere possem et ad tempus redīre
terms.comment: Cicero’s verb for slipping away to a villa or a nearby town and back while something else waits: the day trip itself.

phrases.latin: Crās ad mare excurrēmus; vesperī domum redībimus.
phrases.english: Tomorrow we’ll make a trip to the sea; in the evening we’ll come home again.

phrases.latin: satis erat diērum ut Puteolōs excurrere possem et ad tempus redīre
phrases.english: there would have been days enough for me to run over to Puteoli and be back in time

phrases.latin: an, ut solēbās, intentiōne reī familiāris obeundae crēbrīs excursiōnibus āvocāris?
phrases.english: or are you, as you used to be, called away by frequent trips out, intent on seeing to your estate?

phrases.latin: excursiōnem ad cēnulam subdiālem sūmendam facere

sources: Lewis & Short: excursio · Lewis & Short: excurro
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 53.
